The International Normalized Ratio (INR) is not considered reliable in all situations. While it is widely used as a standard for assessing anticoagulation therapy, different techniques and reagents can lead to discrepancies in results. This inconsistency highlights an issue with standardizing INR testing across various healthcare settings.

Specifically, this study from the UK found that patients who traveled long distances to high-volume centers had improved outcomes compared to those who traveled short distances to low-volume centers. They also reported better 5-year survival rates. These findings suggest that INR may not be reliable when considering patient and hospital factors.

In other words, relying solely on an INR test without taking into account additional variables can lead to inaccurate conclusions about a patient's risk of bleeding or thrombosis. Therefore, it is essential to consider the entire clinical picture, including patient demographics, tumor type, and hospital-specific data, when interpreting INR results.
